Field studies of the Northern crested newt Triturus cristatus in Central European ponds reveal that hatchlings emerge from their gelatinous egg masses at an age of approximately 25 days [ab = approximately 25 days] when water temperatures are maintained at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], reflecting the prolonged embryonic development typical of large-bodied urodeles. The neonate wet weight at birth is remarkably low, estimated at 0.0035 grams [Wwb = 0.0035 grams], a mass that underscores the altricial state of the newly emerged aquatic larva. This initial body size necessitates a substantial period of yolk-sac resorption and early feeding before the tadpole can embark on sustained somatic growth. The jelly-coated eggs themselves are deposited in folded vegetation, a reproductive strategy that provides both physical protection and thermal buffering during the critical early stages of development.

Embryonated eggs and developing larvae of Triturus cristatus experience an aquatic environment that strongly dictates the pace of early life history transitions. Under controlled laboratory conditions set at a constant 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis is approximately 84 days , a period during which the free-swimming larva undergoes profound morphological transformation including limb bud development and gill resorption. This larval duration, equivalent to roughly 2.75 months, is consistent with the moderate pace of development seen in other members of the genus Triturus. The onset of exogenous feeding occurs shortly after yolk-sac resorption, marking the transition to an actively foraging, herbivorous tadpole stage that must accumulate sufficient resources to fuel the energetically costly body plan reorganisation of metamorphic climax.

Sexual maturation in the Northern crested newt is a protracted process that does not occur until well after the terrestrial juvenile stage has been completed. Data from long-term mark-recapture studies indicate that the time since birth at puberty is approximately 600 days [tp = approximately 600 days] when animals are maintained at a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], a relatively late onset of reproductive capacity compared to many smaller-bodied urodeles. The snout-vent length at puberty is approximately 5.44 centimeters [Lp = approximately 5.44 centimeters], a size that indicates attainment of a critical somatic threshold before gametogenesis commences. This delay to maturity likely reflects the energetic demands of achieving the requisite body size and fat reserves necessary to support the substantial reproductive investment that characterises this species, with gravid females directing significant resources toward egg production.

Reproductive output in Triturus cristatus is substantial but constrained by a single annual breeding window. During the spring breeding season at a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], females produce between 70 and 600 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 70 and 600 eggs per clutch], and typically complete between 1 and about 9 clutches each year [F_R_i = between 1 and about 9 clutches each year], reflecting the species' capital-breeding strategy where annual reproductive effort is fuelled by stored reserves accumulated during the previous active season. Adult females in the population attain an ultimate wet weight of 10.6 grams [Wwi = 10.6 grams], while the maximum asymptotic body mass for the species overall has been recorded at 9.4 grams [Wwi = 9.4 grams], a discrepancy that may reflect sexual size dimorphism favouring females who must accommodate developing oocytes. The wet weight at puberty, estimated at 1.35 grams [Wwp = 1.35 grams], represents a substantial increase from the neonatal mass and underscores the extensive growth period required before the first reproductive event.

Longevity and maximum body size data for Triturus cristatus indicate a life history strategy characterised by slow maturation and extended adult survival. The maximum lifespan recorded in wild populations is approximately 10,220 days [am = approximately 10,220 days] when assessed under natural thermal conditions averaging 12 °C [T = 12 °C], equivalent to roughly 28 years, making this one of the longest-lived European urodeles. Males achieve an ultimate snout-vent length of 8.4 centimeters [Li = 8.4 centimeters], whereas the maximum ultimate SVL recorded across both sexes is 10.8 centimeters [Li = 10.8 centimeters], a value derived from total length measurements scaled by a conversion factor. This pronounced size range between sexes and among populations reflects variation in habitat quality, with individuals from productive lowland ponds consistently attaining larger asymptotic dimensions than their counterparts from cooler, oligotrophic upland water bodies.
